Problem 349. Majority rule and a protected right: case 4
Knowledge context.
Democratic procedures use voting, but constitutional systems can place some rights beyond ordinary majority power.
Given facts.

A council of 25 members votes 17 to 8 for a proposal that would forbid one named group from the right to practice a lawful belief. The classroom constitution states: (1) ordinary proposals pass by simple majority; (2) an ordinary majority may not remove the listed equal rights from a group.
Rules.
A decision must satisfy both the voting procedure and the higher rights constraint. Passing a vote is not sufficient if the content violates a protected right.
Task.
Did the proposal receive a majority? May it take effect under the stated constitution?
Step-by-step solution.

1. Vote check: 17>8, so the proposal has a simple majority. 2. Content check: the proposal removes a protected equal right (practice a lawful belief) from a group. 3. The higher rights rule therefore blocks the proposal even though the vote passed.
Answer.
It received a majority, but it may not take effect under the stated rights rule.
Knowledge takeaway.
A majority answers who won a vote; it does not by itself answer whether every possible decision is lawful or fair under higher rules.
Formal model.
Two-stage validity test: procedural predicate AND rights-compliance predicate.

C3. Voting, majority, and quorum
Problem 351. Quorum and majority in a 19-member committee
Knowledge context.
Voting rules often contain more than one threshold. Quorum concerns participation; majority concerns the votes cast according to the stated rule.
Given facts.

A committee has 19 members. 19 are present. Votes: yes=9, no=9, abstain=1. Rule: quorum is at least 60% of all members; if quorum exists, a motion passes when yes votes are strictly more than no votes.
Rules.
First test quorum using all members as the denominator. Only then compare yes and no; abstentions count for presence but not as no votes under this rule.
Task.
Is quorum met, and does the motion pass?
Step-by-step solution.
1. Quorum threshold=ceil(0.60×19)=12. 2. Present=19, so quorum is met. 3. Yes=9, no=9; yes>no is False. 4. Combine the two tests.
Answer.
Quorum is met; the motion does not pass.
Knowledge takeaway.
Procedural reasoning requires applying tests in the right order and using the correct denominator.
Formal model.
